profile.reading:
Switch operates its Atlanta-metro campus, branded "The Keep Campus," at 1 Switch Way, Lithia Springs, Georgia 30122, in Douglas County west of downtown Atlanta; Switch's own Atlanta page does not name Lithia Springs directly, but this OSM record's address tags place it there specifically. Switch's current marketing describes The Keep as a 2,000-plus acre expansion campus with up to 1 million square feet of data center space and up to 150 megawatts of power at this stage, positioned toward "multi-gigawatt capacity upon completion" as the campus continues to build out. Switch announced the Atlanta campus in May 2017, and a November 2020 press release describing an anchor-tenant signing and groundbreaking on the next two buildings gave more granular figures: Building 2 targeted to come online in 2022 at 50 megawatts, and Building 3 targeted for 2023 at 35 megawatts, alongside a stated "$2.5 billion" total expected Georgia investment and hundreds of expected jobs. Switch names Georgia Power by name as its utility partner, describing "100 percent green energy from new, local and renewable energy resources" delivered through that partnership. Georgia Governor Nathan Deal signed House Bill 696, informally called the "Switch Bill," in May 2018, which modernized Georgia's data center sales-and-use tax exemption to extend it to hyperscale colocation facilities with a minimum $250 million investment, a legislative change Switch's own materials credit as enabling this Georgia expansion; Switch's current site states a 0 percent sales and use tax position in Georgia as a result. Switch markets the campus under its self-created "Tier 5 Platinum" certification standard rather than an Uptime Institute Tier rating.

Georgia's data center sector has expanded well beyond the Atlanta metro's historic technology and telecommunications base, with Douglas County's position along Interstate 20 west of Atlanta offering large parcels of developable industrial land and proximity to Georgia Power's regional transmission infrastructure, factors that have drawn Switch and other large-scale operators to the area. Georgia Power's own long-range integrated resource planning has increasingly cited data center and other large-load growth as a driver of future generation and transmission investment across its Georgia service territory, a dynamic playing out alongside the state's continued use of its 2018 data center sales-tax exemption expansion to attract hyperscale-scale investment like Switch's Keep Campus.

reading.body:
The Keep Campus occupies 2,000 acres west of Atlanta in Douglas County, where Switch is building toward multi-gigawatt capacity in phases across up to one million square feet of data center space. The operator currently publishes 150 megawatts of IT load capacity for this stage of expansion. At a typical AI training density of 40 kilowatts per rack, this 150 megawatts translates to roughly 3,750 racks, though the campus is explicitly positioned as an expansion site rather than a finished facility and Switch has announced buildings scheduled for 2022 and 2023 completion. Georgia Power is the utility partner, and Switch markets the campus under its own Tier 5 Platinum certification standard, positioning it for exascale workloads.

This campus ranks fifth among the four facilities in Georgia with published megawatt capacity, accounting for more than double the state's total published data center IT load of 66.3 megawatts. Georgia's 33 mapped data center facilities cluster outside the Atlanta metro along Interstate 20 and near major transmission infrastructure; most publish no capacity figures. The Keep Campus's published 150 megawatts therefore represents the single largest disclosed AI-ready power allocation in the state, though 29 of the 33 mapped Georgia facilities remain opaque on their actual load.

Switch structured its Georgia expansion through House Bill 696, a 2018 state law that exempts hyperscale colocation facilities with a minimum $250 million investment from sales and use tax, a legislative change the operator credits as enabling this build. The campus operates under a stated commitment to 100 percent renewable energy through Georgia Power. The site's position along I-20 west of Atlanta places it near existing regional transmission infrastructure, but neither the operator's published specifications nor the state context provided indicate grid headroom or transmission constraints that might limit future scaling toward the stated multi-gigawatt target.
